verdict.rationale: The canon supplies two patterns the words do not rank. One pattern is kingdom-growth and earth-filling: the mustard-seed (sinapi, G4615) and leaven (zyme, G2219) of Matthew 13:31-33 with the increase verb 'grow' (auxano, G0837, 23 occurrences, regularly used of the word spreading in Acts 6:7, 12:24, 19:20), the Isaiah 11:9 and Habakkuk 2:14 picture of the earth filled ('fill', male, H4390, 235 occurrences) with the knowledge ('knowledge', deah, H1844; 'knowledge', daath, H1847) and glory of the LORD, and the until-clauses of Psalm 110:1 and 1 Corinthians 15:25 marking a reign that culminates in subjugation of enemies. The other pattern is end-time apostasy and difficulty: 2 Timothy 3:1 'difficult times' (chalepoi kairoi; the adjective chalepos, G5467, only twice in the NT), 2 Thessalonians 2:3 'apostasy' or 'falling away' (apostasia, G0646, only twice in the NT), Matthew 24:12 the love of many growing cold ('grow cold', psycho, G5594, a hapax which is a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) as lawlessness ('lawlessness', anomia, G0458) multiplies, and Luke 18:8 questioning whether the Son of Man will find faith. Each pattern is internally coherent, each rests on real recurring vocabulary, and the lexicon does not adjudicate which pattern fixes the trajectory of the age. The pattern is therefore materially contested.

scripture.force: 'All authority' (pasa exousia) in heaven and on earth has been given to the risen Christ. The verse establishes present universal authority but says nothing lexically about the temporal sequence (the timing) of his return relative to any earthly golden age, so it underdetermines (leaves open) the millennial question and is consistent with all three lenses (postmillennial, amillennial, premillennial).

Disciple 'all the nations' (panta ta ethne). The participle 'going' (poreuthentes) plus the aorist (a completed past action form, here used as a command) imperative 'make disciples' (matheteusate) carries a global scope, and a postmillennial reading argues the commission lexically anticipates effective universal discipling within history. But the verb 'make disciples of' (matheteusate) governs 'nations' (ethne) as object without lexically predicting what proportion of each nation ('ethnos') will be discipled, and the commission is consistent with a faithful witness whose ingathered fruit is real but not exhaustive prior to the second coming ('parousia').

Christ promises presence 'until the consummation of the age' (heos tes synteleias tou aionos). The 'until' (heos) clause marks the duration of his presence to the age's end but does not describe a progressively transformed world, leaving the trajectory of the age open.

'Sit' (shev, imperative of 'sit/dwell', yashav) at my right hand 'until' (ad) I make your enemies a footstool. The 'until' (ad) clause sets the session continuing until enemies are subdued, but Hebrew 'until' (ad) marks a terminus only (a stopping point) and does not specify whether the subjugation occurs gradually through the present age (postmillennial reading) or decisively at the end (premillennial or amillennial reading). The lexicon supplies sequence, not mechanism.

'In the latter days' (b'acharit hayamim) the mountain of the LORD's house is established and 'all the nations' (kol hagoyim) stream to it. The verb 'they shall stream/flow' (naharu, qal which is the simple active form of the Hebrew verb 'nahar', flow) pictures nations flowing in, supporting a vision of widespread submission of the nations ('goyim'), but the timeframe relative to Christ's return is not lexically fixed by 'latter' (acharit).

'Many peoples' (ammim rabbim) go up to be taught the 'instruction' or 'law' (torah) of the LORD, which goes out from Zion. The breadth of peoples instructed supports a vision of global gospel reach, yet the passage does not state that this precedes rather than accompanies the consummation (final culmination).

Nations beat 'swords' (charavot) into plowshares and learn 'war' (milchamah) 'no' (lo) more. The picture of universal peace among the nations ('goyim') is concrete, but whether this peace is achieved by progressive gospel triumph before the return or by direct divine judgment at the end is precisely what the words do not settle.

The earth will be 'filled' ('it shall be filled', timmale, niphal which is the Hebrew passive form of 'fill', male, occurring 235 times in the OT) with the 'knowing' (daath, from 'to know', yada, H3045, 860 occurrences) of the 'glory' (kavod) of the LORD as the waters 'cover' (kasah) the sea. The verb 'fill' (male) carries the sense of filling to capacity, and the comparison 'as the waters cover the sea' (ka'asher yekasu al-yam) is a totalizing simile pointing to a universally diffused knowledge of YHWH's glory. A postmillennial reading takes this as a real, in-history pre-second-coming ('pre-parousia') state. The verse fixes the breadth (the whole earth) but not the temporal sequence relative to Christ's return.

'They shall not hurt' (lo yare'u) 'nor destroy' (lo yashchitu) in all my holy mountain, for the 'earth' or 'land' (ha'aretz) shall be 'full' (mal'ah, qal which is the simple active form of the Hebrew verb 'fill', male) of the 'knowledge' (deah, H1844, a noun cognate of 'to know', yada) of the LORD as the waters 'cover' (kasah) the sea. Parallel to Habakkuk 2:14. The construction with 'fill' (male) plus the genitive of content (a noun in the 'of-X' grammatical form, here 'knowledge of the LORD') and the 'all the earth' (kol ha'aretz) scope describes universal saturation; on a postmillennial reading the saturation precedes the return, on the other readings it accompanies or follows it.

The 'kingdom' (basileia) is like a grain of 'mustard' (sinapi, G4615, 5 NT occurrences) which a man takes and sows. 'Mustard' (sinapi) occurs only in this parable (Matthew 13:31, Mark 4:31, Luke 13:19) and in the saying about faith as a grain of mustard ('sinapi') (Matthew 17:20, Luke 17:6). The lexical force is a smallest-to-largest size contrast (the small seed becoming a tree where birds nest). The contrast is real but does not lexically fix WHEN the growth completes (within history before the second coming ('parousia'), on a postmillennial reading, or only at the consummation).

The kingdom is like 'leaven' (zyme, G2219) which a woman 'hid' (enekrupsen, aorist which is a completed past action form of 'hide', enkrupto) in three measures of flour 'until the whole was leavened' (heos hou ezymothe holon). 'Leaven' (zyme) has 13 NT occurrences. Outside this parable the term is consistently negative or corrupting: the 'leaven' (zyme) of the Pharisees and Herod (Matthew 16:6, Matthew 16:11, Matthew 16:12, Mark 8:15, Luke 12:1), and a little 'leaven' (zyme) leavens the whole lump used twice by Paul of corrupting influence (1 Corinthians 5:6, Galatians 5:9, with 1 Corinthians 5:7-8 contrasting old 'leaven' (zyme) of malice with unleavened sincerity). The Matthew 13:33 use is the lone neutral or positive occurrence, where the 'until' (heos) clause points to complete permeation. A postmillennial reading takes the permeation as the future gospel saturation of the world; a counter-reading observes that the same vocabulary elsewhere in the NT describes corruption hidden in dough, which dampens the case from semantic field (range of meaning across uses) alone. The grammar of 'until the whole was leavened' (heos hou ezymothe) gives a terminus (a stopping point) of complete permeation but does not lexically fix that the permeation completes before Christ returns.

'Then the end' (eita to telos), 'whenever' (hotan) he hands the 'kingdom' (basileia) to the Father and abolishes all rule and authority. The adverb 'then/next' (eita) marks the end as a distinct following stage of an ordered sequence (firstfruits, then those of Christ at his coming, then the end in 15:23-24), but it does not describe the prior reign as a progressive earthly transformation rather than a present session (Christ's current heavenly enthronement) terminating at the second coming ('parousia'). 'Then/next' (eita) supplies sequence, not mechanism.

'For he must reign until' (dei gar auton basileuein achri hou the), he must 'reign' (basileuo, G0936, 21 NT occurrences) 'until' (achri) he has put all 'enemies' (echthrous) under his feet. The 'until' (achri) marks the reign continuing up to the subjugation of enemies, echoing Psalm 110:1, but the manner of subjugation (gradual through gospel advance, on a postmillennial reading, or decisive at the end, on the other readings) is not specified, which is the heart of the dispute.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'When the Son of Man comes, will he then find the faith on the earth' (ara ho huios tou anthropou elthon ara heuresei ten pistin epi tes ges). The disjunctive particle 'then/indeed' (ara) introduces a question expecting a doubtful or negative answer, and the future 'he will find' (heuresei) locates the finding at the second coming ('parousia'). The construction does not flatly deny that faith will be found, but it lexically presupposes a state at the return where finding faith is uncertain, which cuts against a uniformly progressive transformation reading. It is acknowledged as a real counterweight that keeps the trajectory lexically open rather than resolving toward triumph.

'And because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of the many will grow cold' (kai dia to plethynthenai ten anomian psygesetai he agape ton pollon), and because 'lawlessness' (anomia, G0458, 16 NT occurrences) 'is multiplied' (plethynthenai, aorist which is a completed past action form passive infinitive of 'multiply', plethyno) the 'love' (agape) of 'the many' (ton pollon) 'will grow cold' (psygesetai, future passive of 'grow cold', psycho, G5594, a NT hapax which is a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible). The hapax 'grow cold' (psycho) is a thermal metaphor of cooling, lexically the strongest single counter-witness to a progressive warming of love across the age. 'Lawlessness' (anomia) paired with 'multiply' (plethyno) depicts increase, not decrease, of lawlessness. The vocabulary depicts a trajectory inverse to what a postmillennial reading expects. It is recognized as a primary complication; one reading reconciles it as a local turbulence within a larger upward trend, but the words themselves point downward.

'Allow both to grow together until the harvest' (aphete synauxanesthai amphotera heos tou therismou), allow both to 'grow together' (synauxanesthai, present indicative which is an ongoing, simple statement of fact passive infinitive of 'grow together', synauxano, a cognate of 'grow', auxano) until the 'harvest' (therismou) at the end of the age. The coexistence of wheat and tares up to the consummation tempers a reading in which evil is progressively eliminated before the return; the same root 'grow' (auxano) that supports kingdom growth here qualifies that growth as parallel to weed growth, not as replacement of it. The leaven simile of Matthew 13:33 cannot be made to carry the postmillennial sense on lexical grounds alone because the immediately preceding parable insists on co-growth.

'In the last days difficult times will come' (en eschatais hemerais enstesontai kairoi chalepoi), in the last days there will 'come' (enstesontai, future middle of 'be present/come upon', enistemi) 'difficult times' (chalepoi kairoi). The adjective 'difficult/harsh' (chalepos, G5467) has only two NT occurrences, the other being Matthew 8:28 of demoniacs as exceedingly dangerous, so its only end-time use is here, with the lexical sense of harsh, hard, perilous. The catalogue that follows (3:2-5) describes moral decline by accumulation of negative-prefixed terms ('lovers of self', philautoi; 'not lovers of good', aphilagathoi; 'unholy', anosioi; 'untaught/savage', apaideutoi). The vocabulary depicts a perilous-last-days trajectory in tension with progressive global transformation. It is addressed as a recognized complication; one reading takes 'difficult times' (chalepoi kairoi) as describing pockets of moral collapse not the global trajectory, but the 'last days' (eschatais hemerais) frame fixes this against the whole last-days era, not an episode within it.

'Unless the apostasy comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed' (ean me elthe he apostasia proton kai apokalyphthe ho anthropos tes anomias). The noun 'apostasy/falling away' (apostasia, G0646) has only 2 NT occurrences, the other (Acts 21:21) accusing Paul of teaching 'apostasy' (apostasia) from Moses, so the eschatological (end-times) sense here is effectively a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible in this sense). The clause makes the 'apostasy' (apostasia) and the 'lawless one' (anomos) figure preconditions of the second coming ('parousia') (the 'day of the Lord', hemera tou kyriou, 2:2), which presupposes a falling-away rather than a triumph immediately before Christ's return. It is acknowledged as a counterweight; a postmillennial reading places the 'apostasy' (apostasia) at the very end of a long age of triumph, but the lexical sequencing ('first', proton) of 'apostasy' (apostasia) before the day of the Lord is a real pressure on a smooth-triumph reading.

'Whenever the thousand years are completed' (otan telesthe ta chilia ete) Satan 'will be loosed' (lythesetai) from his prison and will go out 'to deceive' (planesai) the 'nations' (ta ethne). On any reading that ties the 'thousand years' (chilia ete) to a pre-second-coming ('pre-parousia') gospel age, this final loosing of Satan to deceive the nations again describes a sharp end-of-age reversal of the kingdom-saturation pattern. It is not resolved here because the analysis of Revelation 20 vocabulary is carried in the sibling amillennialism and premillennialism evidence files, and a full canon traversal of 'deceive' (planao) and the 'whenever' (otan) clause sequencing was not redone in this pass.

variants.note: The cited Matthean and Pauline verses carry minor apparatus marks (notes in the critical edition of New Testament textual variants, for example the relative pronoun in 1 Corinthians 15:25 and verb forms in Matthew 28:19-20 and Matthew 13:33), but none of these readings shift the temporal-sequence question that the proposition turns on. Revelation 20 and 2 Thessalonians 2 are outside the open-cbgm 3 John sample, so CBGM (a computer-assisted method for evaluating textual variants) data was not consulted and ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) status is treated as shadow.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the kingdom-growth parables of Matthew 13 (mustard seed 'sinapi', leaven 'zyme', with 'grow' (auxano) of word-spread in Acts 6:7 and 12:24 and 19:20) together with the earth-filled-with-knowledge oracles of Habakkuk 2:14 and Isaiah 11:9 ('fill' (male) plus 'knowledge' (daath) or 'knowledge' (deah) of YHWH, 'cover' (kasah)-the-sea simile of total saturation), the streaming of nations in Isaiah 2:2-4 ('they shall stream' (naharu), 'all the nations' (kol hagoyim)), and the reign-until-enemies of Psalm 110:1 and 1 Corinthians 15:25 ('until' (ad), 'until' (achri)) as a single trajectory of gospel triumph that progressively transforms the world before Christ returns. On this reading the apostasy texts describe localized final-stage reversal, not the trajectory of the whole age, and Revelation 20's binding of Satan is the present-age restraint on deceiving the nations that lexically enables the gospel saturation.

Takes Psalm 110:1 and 1 Corinthians 15:25 as the present heavenly session (Christ's current reign at God's right hand) in which Christ already reigns until the second coming ('parousia'), with the kingdom advancing spiritually while wheat and tares coexist (Matthew 13:30 'grow together' (synauxanesthai)) until a single end. The Isaiah 2 and Habakkuk 2 oracles are read as the consummated new creation, not a pre-second-coming ('pre-parousia') stage. The kingdom-growth parables describe the kingdom's real but mixed advance in the present age, not a future earthly golden epoch. On this lens the until-clauses do not require a transformed world before the return, and the proposition is denied.

Reads 'then the end' (eita to telos) and the subjugation of enemies as occurring at and after the second coming ('parousia'), with the golden age of Isaiah 2:2-4, Habakkuk 2:14, and Isaiah 11:9 located in a post-return reign rather than achieved by gospel triumph beforehand. The apostasy texts (2 Timothy 3:1 'difficult times' (chalepoi kairoi), 2 Thessalonians 2:3 'apostasy' (apostasia), Matthew 24:12 'lawlessness' (anomia) 'multiply' (plethyno) and 'love' (agape) 'grow cold' (psycho)) describe the end of the present age, not the eschatological (end-times) end of a triumphant epoch. On this lens Christ returns before, not after, the age of universal peace, so the proposition is denied.

Locates the Isaiah 2 peace and Habakkuk 2 earth-filled knowledge in a future earthly millennial kingdom inaugurated by Christ's return, and reads the present age as ending in 'apostasy' (apostasia) (2 Thessalonians 2:3) rather than triumph. The Great Commission is discipling without a guarantee of worldwide transformation before the second coming ('parousia'), and the kingdom parables describe the church age's mixed character rather than its progressive conquest. On this lens the proposition is denied.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the covenantal and eschatological (end-times) arc connecting Psalm 110, Isaiah 2, Habakkuk 2, Isaiah 11, the Great Commission, the kingdom parables, and 1 Corinthians 15, hence the redemptive-historical method (reading Scripture as a unified unfolding story of salvation). The same Hebrew and Greek terms ('until' (ad), 'until' (achri), 'then/next' (eita), 'they shall stream' (naharu), 'fill' (male), 'leaven' (zyme), 'mustard' (sinapi), 'grow' (auxano)) sustain mutually exclusive sequence readings, and the apostasy vocabulary ('difficult/harsh' (chalepos), 'apostasy' (apostasia), 'lawlessness' (anomia), 'grow cold' (psycho)) supplies a real second canonical pattern. The lexicon alone does not adjudicate between the frameworks. Each lens above is stated in its strongest lexical form so a reader holding any one is fairly represented.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Scripture describes the temporal relationship between Christ's return, the subjugation of his enemies, and any age of widespread gospel peace among the nations, and whether that peace is achieved before or at the second coming ('parousia').
stem_audit.notes: The original stem embeds the postmillennial thesis as a premise by asserting an extended age of gospel triumph in which the kingdom progressively transforms the world and placing Christ's return after it. The phrases 'progressively transforms' and 'after an extended age of gospel triumph' presuppose the very sequence and mechanism in dispute. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form states the underlying question without assuming the outcome. VERDICT-CHANGED: no, the verdict is unchanged from the prior file. Deepening over the prior file added a second canonical pattern ('difficult/harsh' (chalepos), 'apostasy' (apostasia), 'lawlessness' (anomia), 'grow cold' (psycho)) to balance the kingdom-growth pattern ('mustard' (sinapi), 'leaven' (zyme), 'grow' (auxano), 'fill' (male), 'knowledge' (daath), 'glory' (kavod)) symmetrically, ran direct canon-distribution queries for the load-bearing lemmas (the dictionary forms of key words), and harmonized the three-lens framing with sibling doc-amillennialism and doc-premillennialism (each there also disputed, low confidence).

lay_summary: This proposition asks whether Christ returns only after a long age in which the gospel gradually transforms the whole world into a kingdom of peace. The honest answer from the words alone is that the canon supplies two real patterns and does not rank them. The first pattern is kingdom-growth. The mustard-seed (sinapi) parable and the leaven (zyme) parable (Matthew 13:31-33) picture a small beginning that ends with a whole leavened lump or a tree where birds nest, and the verb for grow (auxano) is the same verb the book of Acts uses for the word of God increasing (6:7, 12:24, 19:20). Habakkuk 2:14 and Isaiah 11:9 say the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea, where the Hebrew word for fill (male) carries the sense of filling to capacity. Psalm 110:1 and 1 Corinthians 15:25 say the Messiah reigns until enemies are subdued. Read together these supply a vision of expanding, victorious kingdom. The second pattern is apostasy and difficulty at the end. 2 Timothy 3:1 calls the last days difficult or perilous (chalepos, the adjective occurs only twice in the New Testament). 2 Thessalonians 2:3 says the day of the Lord does not come unless the apostasia, the falling away, comes first (the noun also occurs only twice). Matthew 24:12 says lawlessness (anomia) will be multiplied and the love of many will grow cold (psycho is a New Testament hapax, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, used only here). Luke 18:8 asks whether the Son of Man will find faith on the earth at his coming. Read together these supply a vision of end-time reversal. The until-words (ad in Hebrew, achri in Greek) in Psalm 110:1 and 1 Corinthians 15:25 mark a terminus without saying whether the subjugation arrives slowly or suddenly. The leaven (zyme) of Matthew 13:33 carries unambiguous gospel-saturation force here, but every other New Testament use of the same word is corrupting influence (the leaven of the Pharisees, a little leaven leavens the whole lump), which dampens any argument from semantic field alone. Both patterns are internally coherent, both rest on real recurring vocabulary, and the lexicon does not adjudicate. The lexical evidence is therefore genuinely contested rather than decisive.
